technical: The post plays down the Java agent attach timeouts and treats a libinstrument mapping as proof the helper attached. The log shows attach timeouts for two different PIDs, which is probably both JVMs. Fix: Match PIDs 388 and 409 to orders and inventory, for example with the 'instrumenting process' log lines. Then say plainly how many JVMs timed out. Rename the measure to 'agent library loaded', not 'attached'. Add one sentence explaining that the HTTP map and traces don't depend on this helper, while Java TLS capture does.

technical: The post recommends a second value for joined traces, but a run with the first value alone was never measured, so nothing shows that value is required. Fix: Rerun the case with only the first value, using a longer trace wait (for example 300 s) and a retry pass, and report joined of found. Or reword the advice as 'With both values, 39 of 39 found traces joined across nodes. I did not measure the first value alone.' and drop the suggestion that it fails without the second value.

editorial: The brief's takeaway promised a measured answer to 'whether traces across nodes need a second value'. That answer is missing, and the TL;DR shows the 39/39 result without saying the baseline is missing. Fix: Add to the TL;DR: 'The first value alone wasn't measured for traces; see below.' Or run the baseline and report both numbers side by side.

editorial: The structure and phrasing look generated: templated headings, bold labels and stock transitions. Fix: Rename the sections after what happened ('Turning on OBI with chart 0.163.1', 'Same pod UIDs before and after'). Cut the bold labels from the TL;DR and vary the sentence rhythm. Fix the time to match the run: 26.9 minutes for the scripts, plus Terraform.

The Java helper section plays down the evidence. 05-fix.log:29 and :33 show 'java attach timed out' for two different PIDs (388 and 409), which looks like both JVMs. The post says 'at least one'. jvm_helper_attached=1 only counts libinstrument mappings, so it does not show that the agent finished attaching.

The trace comparison with the first value alone was never measured: 0 of 56 IDs came back within 90 s. The post admits this, but the 'Use it' section still implies that joined traces need the second value.

Latency is handled honestly. The -1.06 ms median comes with overlapping ranges and is reported as no visible change. The '28 minutes' in the TL;DR doesn't match the step times, which add up to 24 minutes, or the 26.9-minute run.
The reader and their decision are clear, and the opening delivers what the title promises: services on the map, no restarts.

The finding beyond the docs is thin. The docs already say no restart is needed. The new parts are the UID-level proof on Amazon Linux 2023, the 39 of 39 cross-node join with propagation on, and the attach timeouts. The one comparison that would answer the brief, with and without propagation, is missing.

It reads as templated. Bold labels ('What you get / The trick / The proof') appear in the TL;DR and again as section headings ('The trick', 'The proof'), along with stock lines like 'Here's what one value gives you' and 'That's the whole change.'
The trade-offs on privileges, namespaces and agents are covered honestly, and the 'What I didn't test' section is good.
Demand is weak. The only signal is one OBI issue with two comments, and it is about Java agent injection into non-root JVMs, not first service maps. There is no search or traffic data.
The title is in practitioner language and gives Splunk and the chart credit for the result, which suits a platform engineer looking for an EKS service map.
Splunk fits naturally here and isn't forced. OBI and the Splunk chart are the subject of the post.

claims.text: OBI is a beta feature in Splunk Observability Cloud
OBI runs as a DaemonSet and captures traces and request metrics from running workloads with no code change or restart
The chart turns OBI on with obi.enabled=true and runs it privileged with host PID and host network, and also documents a reduced capability set
The chart guide names Ubuntu as its tested node OS
OBI outgoing propagation is off by default
Proxies and load balancers can affect propagation
Async frameworks need their own context-propagation check
Splunk recommends combining OBI with language agents, and OBI skips processes that already have OpenTelemetry instrumentation
Reducing OBI's capabilities affects Java agent injection into non-root JVMs
A language agent gives the deepest detail, joins the JVM at startup, and so requires pods to roll
A first map showing who calls whom is often enough to choose which teams to talk to next
Joined cross-node traces need the second (propagation) value

brief.reader: Platform engineer running Java services on EKS who wants a first service map before asking any team to change a deployment
brief.decision: Whether to turn on OBI through the Splunk OTel Collector chart as a first layer across a cluster, before rolling out language agents
brief.question: Can I get services that are already running on EKS onto the Splunk APM map without restarting a pod, and what do I get from it?
brief.takeaway: You can decide from measured numbers: what one Helm value puts on the map for running services, what it does to the pods, and whether traces across nodes need a second value.
brief.adds: Existing pages state that OBI needs no restart and list what it captures. This post measures it on EKS on Amazon Linux 2023: services on the map, each pod's UID and restart count before and after, whether one trace spans two nodes with and without propagation, the Java helper OBI loads, and the p95 latency added.
brief.open_question: With obi.enabled=true alone on chart 0.163.1, how many running services reach the Splunk APM map, how many pod restarts does it add, and how many services share one trace across two nodes with and without outgoing header propagation?
tradeoffs: OBI first for a broad map, or a language agent for deeper framework detail
A privileged DaemonSet with host PID and host network, or the chart's documented reduced capabilities
Every namespace by default, or a namespace filter
Outgoing header propagation on, or kept at its default
